prompt:
I need the front end for Tillbird. A free personal money app with millions of everyday users that links their bank and card accounts, and lets them hand its built-in AI assistant a savings goal to work out, then check and approve the plan it comes back with.

Who's using it: Priya Raman, 29, a ward nurse in Leeds who uses Tillbird mostly to see her balance on payday. She has no budgeting background, doesn't know the difference between a standing order and a direct debit, and has never used the assistant for anything bigger than 'how much did I spend on takeaways'.

What they're doing right now: Twenty minutes ago she asked the assistant: 'Help me save £1,200 for Mei's wedding in Lisbon by 1 May without touching my rent.' It has finished a first pass. It re-sorted three months of her transactions into categories, found nine recurring charges, and proposed a weekly saving of £52 made up of five changes, including cancelling a £34.99 gym membership it labels 'unused'. She knows she went to that gym twice last week; the charge just shows up under the leisure centre's parent company name. Before she accepts anything, she needs to see what each suggestion is based on, correct the assistant where it got her life wrong, ask it to redo the numbers without the gym cut, and decide whether the revised plan is believable. Then she'll accept it and set up the automatic transfer to her savings pot.

What's in the system at this point: Two linked accounts: Monzo-style current account (balance £847.20) and a credit card (£312.55 owed, £2,000 limit). 418 transactions from 1 Aug–20 Nov 2026. 61 of them were re-categorised by the assistant, each with its old and new category and a confidence level. Nine recurring charges: Netflix £10.99, Spotify £11.99, Everyone Active (billed as 'SLM Leisure') £34.99, iCloud £2.99, Vinted Pro £4.00, phone contract £22, Headspace £49.99/yr, a council tax direct debit £143, and a charity donation £8. The assistant's draft plan has five proposed changes, each with an estimated weekly saving, the specific transactions it cites, and a status of proposed, accepted, rejected or revised. The goal is £1,200 by 1 May 2026 (23 weeks away). Rent of £675 on the 1st is marked protected. A history of the assistant's two drafts so far shows what changed between them and why.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
